transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, doctor. I guess... I mean, my supervisor said I needed to come in and get checked out, but if you want to know what actually brings me in, it goes back to our staff meeting on Tuesday. We always have these mandatory meetings in the big break room down at the facility where I work—I'm a personal care aide, you see, so we deal with a lot of older folks. And fall prevention is just... it's huge. It's the most important thing we do, because if somebody goes down, it's a whole mess of paperwork and ambulances and it's just bad. 

Anyway, we were all sitting there, and the manager was talking about protocols, and I just got so... I don't know, worked up? Like, the energy was just buzzing right through my chest and I felt like they weren't explaining it right or taking it seriously enough. So I just stood up. I had to show them how it actually happens on the floor. I started acting out this whole fall-prevention drill right there in the middle of the room. I grabbed a couple of the folding chairs—the heavy grey metal ones—and I was dragging them around to show the angles of the beds, and my arms were just waving everywhere, demonstrating how you have to hook under their arms and block their momentum with your knee. 

And the thing is... I just kept going. I couldn't seem to stop. My supervisor, Brenda, she was saying, "Okay, we get it, please sit down," and a couple of the other folks were telling me to sit down and take a breath, but I just couldn't. It was like my brain and my body just had to finish the whole routine, moving the chairs and waving around, even though everyone was just staring at me like I was crazy. I just couldn't turn the motor off, you know? So... yeah. That's why they told me I had to come see you.
Over the past several days, have you found yourself needing much less sleep than usual without feeling tired?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because sleep has just been... it's been completely different lately. I mean, usually I'm the kind of guy who needs a solid seven or eight hours, especially with the physical work I do, lifting folks and being on my feet all day. But for the last, oh, maybe four or five days? It's like someone just flipped a switch in my head. 

I'll go to bed around, say, midnight, after tossing and turning and trying to wind down, and then boom—two, maybe three hours later, my eyes just snap open. And I don't mean waking up groggy and reaching for the snooze button. I mean wide awake, completely energized, like I just drank a pot of coffee. It'll be 3:00 AM, pitch black outside, the whole house is dead silent, and I'm just lying there thinking, "Well, I'm up, let's get the day started!" 

And I don't feel tired at all. That's the crazy part. I'll get out of bed, go into the kitchen, maybe start making a list of things I need to do at work, or reorganizing the pantry, or sketching out these ideas I have for better wheelchair ramps... just making all these plans while it's still dark out. And I honestly don't even think twice about it. It just feels perfectly normal to be up and running on two hours of sleep. I don't drag during the day, I don't need a nap... my motor just keeps running and running. So, yeah, I guess you could say I've been needing a whole lot less sleep.

I'm 41 now, and I've been doing personal care for a long time, and you see a lot of things, you know? You see people go through all sorts of phases. 

But for me, personally? I don't know. I guess I've always just been me. Sometimes I have more energy, sometimes I have less, but I can't really pinpoint a specific time that stands out like what's happening right now. This whole not sleeping thing, and the energy in my chest... this feels pretty new, or at least, a lot more intense than anything I remember. But maybe I'm not understanding what you're getting at. What kind of period were you going to ask about before you stopped? Because I can tell you all about the time I worked at the facility over in Westside, back in '15, and we had a whole month where everything was just upside down... but I don't know if that's what you mean.

Experienced... wait, you mean like feeling down? Like a real low period, like depression? Because if that's what you're getting at, honestly, no. I mean, don't get me wrong, I'm a human being, I get sad just like anybody else. Like back in 2018 when my dog Buster passed away—he was this scruffy little terrier mix, smartest dog you ever met—I was pretty torn up about that for a few days. But as far as a whole long period where I just can't function or get out of bed? No, never anything like that. 

I've always been a worker, you know? I'm the guy who picks up the slack. You can ask anyone down at the facility, they'll tell you I'm the one who always shows up, rain or shine. Even when things get really tough, like last winter when we had this awful stomach bug sweep through the entire memory care unit—oh man, that was a nightmare, we were short-staffed and everyone was getting sick—but I still came in every single day. I just keep moving. I don't really get stuck in those dark places that some people talk about. 

I mean, I know what it looks like. I see it in the residents sometimes, especially the ones whose families never come to visit. They just kind of give up, they stare at the wall, they won't even touch their peach cobbler on Sundays. It breaks your heart to see it. But for me, personally? No. I've never had a time where I felt completely hopeless or couldn't drag myself to work. So if you're looking for some time in my past where I was down in the dumps for weeks on end, I really don't have anything like that to tell you.
Have you recently used any stimulants, such as recreational drugs, prescription pills, or over-the-counter energy supplements?

Stimulants? Like drugs or pills? Oh, no, absolutely not. I mean, I'm a personal care aide, you know? I'm responsible for people's lives, their safety. I can't be messing around with stuff like that. I've never touched recreational drugs in my life. I don't even like taking Tylenol unless my back is really, really screaming at me after a long shift of lifting folks out of their wheelchairs. 

And as for energy supplements, you mean like those little shots they sell at the gas station? The ones that look like tiny bottles of antifreeze? No way. I see the younger guys at work chugging those things, or those huge cans of energy drinks that smell like battery acid and fruit punch, and I just shake my head. I tell them, "You're gonna burn a hole right through your stomach with that garbage." 

I don't need any of that. Like I was saying before, I usually just drink coffee. Just regular old drip coffee. And honestly, lately, with all this energy I've been having, I haven't even been finishing my morning cup. I'll pour it, take two sips, and then I'm just off and running, doing a million things at once. I don't need a pill or a powder to get me going. It's just coming from inside me right now. So, no, definitely no stimulants or anything like that. Just me, running on my own engine, I guess you could say.
